about: Civil Engineering Design 1 (CIVE40002) is a 7.5-ECTS core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Civil Engineering, running in the autumn and spring terms. It is the first of the design modules, which Imperial says are co-taught by leading consultants. Students work in groups on problem-based design through two intensive Creative Design weeks: sketching, hands-on and parametric modelling, critique, and a full-scale (1:1) build. There is no published lecture syllabus or assessment breakdown, so this is a guide pack built from the module description. It explains how the module works and covers the skills and quick structural checks you will use.

notes.body:
An Imperial news article from March 2021 described the first-year sketching and modelling course in civil engineering, as it was run that year. The details may have changed since.

What it described (2020–21)
- Sketching is used as the first step in generating ideas.
- Groups of five or six build paper models from their sketches; the stages included designing a pop-up model.
- The structures are then recreated digitally, using Rhino and Grasshopper for parametric design.
- Groups write visual build instructions for their models.

The current module record adds giving and receiving critical feedback and reflecting on the engineer's role as designer and maker (topic 4).

Why engineers sketch
A sketch is the fastest way to explore an idea and to explain it to someone else. Good design sketches:
- start from light construction lines, "crating" the object in a box before adding detail;
- use simple pictorial views (isometric, oblique, or quick perspective), plus plans and elevations where those are clearer;
- are annotated with arrows showing loads and how they reach the ground, key dimensions, and the material intended;
- are produced in quantity. Many quick alternatives beat one careful drawing early in a project.

Why build physical models
- A model shows immediately whether something stands up, how it deflects and where it is floppy. It reveals stability problems that are easy to miss on paper.
- It communicates form to a client far better than a drawing.
- Paper and card behave like thin plates: weak in bending out of plane, but stiff when folded or curved. This is the same principle as profiled steel decking or a folded-plate roof. Folding and curving are the main tools for making paper models stiff.

Scale effects
A small model is not a reliable guide to strength at full size. If every length is scaled by a factor s:
- self-weight scales with s³ (volume);
- cross-sectional area scales with s²;
- so the stress due to self-weight scales with s.

At 1:10 scale, self-weight stresses are a tenth of full scale. A model that easily carries its own weight therefore says little about whether the full structure will. Stability and the form of a structure transfer well between scales; strength must be checked by calculation.

How to prepare
- Spend ten minutes a day sketching real structures, such as bridges, canopies and roof trusses, and mark their load paths.
- Practise cutting and folding paper to see how much stiffness folds and curves add.

notes.h: Conceptual structural design and quick checks
notes.body:
In the design weeks you will choose a structural concept quickly and then check that it is feasible. The basic questions are always the same.

1. Where are the loads, and how do they get to the ground?
Trace the load path: deck, to beams, to columns or hangers, to foundations. Each element should have a clear job.
- Tension members (ties, cables, hangers) can be slender, because they cannot buckle.
- Compression members (struts, columns, arches) must be stocky or braced, because they can buckle.
- Bending members (beams, slabs) work most efficiently when they are deep, because a deeper section has much more stiffness and strength for the same amount of material.

2. Is it stable?
- A structure needs bracing in every direction it can sway.
- Triangles are rigid; a rectangle of pin-jointed members is a mechanism unless it is braced or its joints are rigid.
- Check stability under sideways loads (wind, people leaning) as well as under gravity.

3. Will it carry the load? Quick checks
- Simply supported beam under a uniform load w over span L: maximum moment M = wL²/8 at midspan, maximum shear V = wL/2 at the supports, and midspan deflection δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI).
- Pin-ended strut: Euler buckling load Pcr = π²EI/L². Doubling the length cuts the buckling load to a quarter.
- Bending stress: σ = M/Z, with Z = bh²/6 for a rectangle. Doubling the depth gives four times the bending capacity and eight times the stiffness (I = bh³/12).

Design loads (Eurocodes)
UK structural design uses the Eurocodes. BS EN 1990 sets the basis of design.
- For the ultimate limit state, the recommended factors in expression 6.10 are 1.35 on permanent actions (Gk) and 1.5 on the leading variable action (Qk), so the design load is 1.35Gk + 1.5Qk.
- BS EN 1990 also offers the pair 6.10a and 6.10b (use whichever is larger), and the UK National Annex allows either route. With the UK values, 6.10a is 1.35Gk + 1.5ψ0Qk and 6.10b is 0.925 × 1.35Gk (about 1.25Gk) + 1.5Qk, which usually gives a slightly lower design load than 6.10.

Worked example
A beam spans 4 m, simply supported, with Gk = 3.0 kN/m and Qk = 2.0 kN/m.
- Design load w = 1.35 × 3.0 + 1.5 × 2.0 = 7.05 kN/m.
- Mmax = 7.05 × 4²/8 = 14.1 kNm.
- Vmax = 7.05 × 4/2 = 14.1 kN. (Mmax and Vmax happen to be numerically equal here only because L/4 = 1 m.)
- Using unfactored loads would give 10.0 kNm, which is unsafe for an ultimate check. Swapping the factors gives 14.4 kNm.
- For comparison, with ψ0 = 0.7 the 6.10a/6.10b route gives 6.15 and 6.75 kN/m, so w = 6.75 kN/m and Mmax = 13.5 kNm, slightly less than with 6.10.

How to prepare
- Be fluent with wL²/8, wL/2, 5wL⁴/384EI and π²EI/L².
- Practise sketching bending moment diagrams for simple cases.
- When you present a concept, show the load path and one or two quick checks. Clients and tutors want to see that you know why it stands up.

notes.h: Digital and parametric modelling, critique and reflection
notes.body:
The module record includes applying geometric and parametric modelling, giving and receiving critical feedback, and reflecting on the civil engineer's role as designer and maker. These are skills you will use in every later design project.

Parametric modelling
- In a parametric model, the geometry is generated by rules from a few input parameters, such as span, depth, number of panels or curvature. Changing a parameter regenerates the whole design.
- This lets a team explore many variations quickly, and link the geometry to simple performance measures such as total length of members or approximate weight.
- Visual programming tools such as Grasshopper (inside Rhino) were reported for the first-year sketching and modelling course in 2021. Your year may use different software. The principles are the same.
- Good practice: name your parameters and give them sensible ranges. Keep the logic readable, so a teammate can follow it. Save versions so you can step back if something goes wrong.

From model to making
- Digital models can produce cutting patterns, the dimensions of every piece and assembly sequences. These are essential for a full-scale build.
- Plan the build like a small construction project: a list of parts and materials, a sequence, team roles, temporary support while it is incomplete, and safety (stability during erection, lifting, tool use).

Giving and receiving critique
Design reviews ("crits") are a normal part of professional practice.
When giving feedback:
- start from the brief: does the design answer it?
- be specific. "The cantilever looks unstable under sideways load because there is no bracing" is useful; "I don't like it" is not;
- suggest an improvement or a question to test.

When receiving feedback:
- listen, take notes and ask questions to understand the point;
- separate the idea from yourself;
- decide what to act on and record why.

Peer feedback works best when it is anonymous and structured around the assessment criteria.

Reflection
Reflective writing is not a diary. A common structure is:
- what happened;
- what you thought or felt about it;
- what you learned from it (link to theory or to feedback received);
- what you will do differently next time.

Be honest about what went wrong and specific about what you would change. Tie it to the civil engineer's role as both designer and maker.

How to prepare
Keep notes throughout each design week: decisions, failures, feedback and how you responded. Writing the reflection is then quick and authentic.

questions.q: A 1:10 scale model of a footbridge, made of the same material as the real structure, carries its own weight easily. Compared with the full-size bridge, the stress due to self-weight in the model is:
questions.why: Self-weight scales with volume (1/1000) and the cross-sectional area that resists it scales with 1/100, so the stress due to self-weight scales with 1/10. Saying it is the same ignores the fact that weight and area scale differently. One hundredth is just the scaling of area. One thousandth is just the scaling of weight (volume). Neither on its own gives the stress.

questions.q: A simply supported beam spans 4 m and carries Gk = 3.0 kN/m and Qk = 2.0 kN/m. Using 1.35Gk + 1.5Qk, what is the maximum design bending moment?
questions.why: w = 1.35 × 3.0 + 1.5 × 2.0 = 7.05 kN/m, so M = wL²/8 = 7.05 × 16/8 = 14.1 kNm. 10.0 kNm uses the unfactored load of 5 kN/m. 14.4 kNm swaps the factors, putting 1.5 on the permanent load and 1.35 on the imposed load. 28.2 kNm uses wL²/4, which is the formula for a central point load of wL, not a uniform load.

questions.q: A slender pin-ended strut in a model is replaced by one of the same section but twice as long. Its Euler buckling load becomes:
questions.why: Pcr = π²EI/L², so doubling L divides the load by 2² = 4. Half the original would follow if Pcr varied with 1/L, which is the wrong power. Unchanged would follow only for a short, stocky member that crushes rather than buckles, and the question says it is slender. Buckling capacity cannot increase with length.

questions.q: For a simple footbridge concept (a deck on two beams spanning between abutments), describe the load path and identify one check for each main element.
markScheme: People and deck self-weight load the deck, which spans across to the two main beams
Beams carry the load in bending to the abutments: check bending (M = wL²/8 with factored loads) and deflection (5wL⁴/384EI)
Beam ends deliver shear (V = wL/2) and bearing forces to the abutments
Abutments and foundations carry the reactions into the ground: check bearing and stability
Lateral stability: bracing between the beams or a stiff deck against sway and lateral-torsional effects
questions.modelAnswer: Pedestrian loads and the deck's own weight act on the deck, which spans across to the two main beams. The beams carry the load along the span in bending to the abutments at each end. For each beam, I would check the bending moment at midspan (M = wL²/8, using factored loads such as 1.35Gk + 1.5Qk) against its capacity, the shear at the supports (V = wL/2), and the deflection under service loads (5wL⁴/384EI), since bounce and sag matter for users. The beam ends deliver their reactions to the abutments, which pass the load into the ground through their foundations. These need checks on bearing pressure and stability against sliding or overturning if they also retain soil. Finally, the beams need lateral bracing, either from a stiff deck or from cross-bracing, so the bridge cannot sway and the compression flanges cannot buckle sideways.
